one_line.text: Harvard legal scholar, among the most-cited in his field, who ran the US regulatory office and turned Nudge's ideas into federal practice.

biography.text: Born in 1954, Sunstein built a career at Chicago and Harvard Law as one of the most-cited legal scholars alive, writing across constitutional law, regulation, and behavioural policy at a famously industrial pace. From 2009 to 2012 he ran the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, where cost-benefit review met the choice-architecture ideas he and Thaler had published the year before — making him the rare co-author who personally operationalised the book. His dozens of books extend the programme from conformity and group polarisation to noise (with Kahneman) and the ethics of influence.

background.text: He supplies the book's legal-policy half: where Thaler brings the anomalies, Sunstein brings the regulatory machinery — disclosure design, default-setting authority, and the administrative law of steering people lawfully.

expertise.text: Constitutional and administrative law, regulation, and behavioural public policy, with government practice at the highest level to match the scholarship.

perspective_and_limits.text: Sunstein is the libertarian-paternalism idea's tireless defender, which makes him an interested judge of its critics; the paternalism and manipulation objections documented against the programme are, in large part, objections to positions he has spent two decades advancing.
